A.biggest_strength: Visually maps sequence and acknowledgment numbers directly onto interactive byte-stream strips with sliding SND.NXT/RCV.NXT pointers and a color-coded unifying formula (ack = seq + len + SYN + FIN) that intuitively demonstrates why SYN and FIN consume sequence space.
A.biggest_weakness: Uses fixed initial sequence numbers and payload values rather than allowing arbitrary user-inputted ISNs and payload sizes.

B.biggest_strength: Provides interactive customization controls allowing students to enter custom ISNs, modify payload byte lengths, generate random 32-bit ISNs, and toggle Wireshark-style relative sequence numbers.
B.biggest_weakness: Severely degraded mobile experience where a 480px min-width SVG causes horizontal overflow that cuts off the entire server column on phone viewports, paired with visuals that rely on text cards rather than visualizing the underlying byte-stream mechanism.

structured_output.reasons: Page A is the clear winner because it visualizes the actual underlying mechanism of TCP sequence and acknowledgment numbers rather than just displaying numbers in text cards next to a standard ladder diagram. By showing byte-level sequence strips with active SND.NXT and RCV.NXT pointers alongside the color-coded formula ack = seq + len + SYN + FIN, a networking student immediately understands why SYN and FIN consume sequence space while pure ACKs do not. Furthermore, Page A features exceptional responsive design that adapts its SVG viewBox and tables seamlessly to phone viewports, whereas Page B completely cuts off the server column on mobile screens.
